claims.text: Martensitic stainless steel can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition as tempering temperature increases.
The proposed starting material is quenched and hardened martensitic stainless steel.
The transition occurs over a critical temper-embrittlement temperature window.
Impurity segregation at grain boundaries causes the tempering-induced transition.
At intermediate tempering temperatures, phosphorus, antimony, or arsenic can diffuse to and concentrate at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary enrichment by phosphorus, antimony, or arsenic induces embrittlement.
At lower tempering temperatures, impurity diffusion is minimal.
At higher tempering temperatures, recovery processes reduce impurity segregation.
Reduced segregation at higher tempering temperatures restores ductility.
Increasing tempering temperature produces ductile behavior, then brittle behavior, and finally recovered ductile behavior.
Quenched martensitic stainless steel remains ductile under low-temperature tempering conditions when significant impurity diffusion is absent.
The proposed behavior is expected in conventional alloys containing segregating impurities.
The proposed behavior is not expected in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys.
Disrupted diffusion paths in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys prevent the proposed transition.
The transition temperature range and magnitude of mechanical-property changes depend on alloy composition and impurity concentration.
